tldr: By building CoRP, a compact policy with just 48.9M parameters and no VLM or video-generative priors, this work shows that manipulation success is largely driven not by model scale, but by visual representations that are pretrained, task-adapted, and token-compressed.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of CoRP (a) and performance comparison across key benchmarks (b). By compressing visual features with a resampler and generating actions with a 1-block DiT, this compact 48.9M-parameter design matches the success rates of state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs that are tens to over a hundred times larger.
overview:
In multi-task robot manipulation, billion-parameter vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) with video-generative priors currently dominate the spotlight. However, existing systems vary model scale, architecture, pretrained priors, and training datasets all at once. As a result, what actually drives their performance gains has remained a black box.

The authors hypothesize that most manipulation performance comes from the quality of the visual representation, while massive parameter scale and video-generative priors are largely incidental. To test this, they build CoRP (Compressed Representation Policy), a deliberately compact policy with only 48.9M parameters that uses neither a VLM nor a video-generative prior.

CoRP holds the action generator fixed while systematically varying extractor properties one at a time: encoder initialization, fine-tuning versus freezing, token compression methods, and the necessity of language conditioning. In experiments, it achieves a 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and 75.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, matching or surpassing systems up to 163× larger.

Detailed ablation studies reveal three essentials for a compact policy to succeed: the representation must be pretrained, adapted (fine-tuned) to robot tasks, and compressed to task-relevant tokens via language. Furthermore, language conditioning proves decisive only when visual observations leave the goal ambiguous; it is completely unnecessary when the goal is already obvious from the scene.
contributions: Proposed CoRP, a compact 48.9M-parameter policy with no VLM or video-generative prior, matching the performance of models up to 163× larger.
Demonstrated through rigorous ablations with a fixed action generator that high-performing compact policies require visual representations that are pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed.
Showed that language conditioning functions primarily to disambiguate visually ambiguous goals rather than providing broad general knowledge.
Validated real-world transfer using the exact same compact architecture on a dual-arm robot across tasks requiring disturbance recovery, coordinated placement, and precision plug insertion.

sections.heading: Where Does the True Power of Giant Models Come From?
sections.summary: To disentangle which components drive the success of recent VLAs and WAMs, the authors build a deliberately compact policy, CoRP. They hypothesize that manipulation performance hinges on visual representations rather than parameter scale, testing this through controlled comparisons.
sections.details:
In robot manipulation, vision-language-action models (VLAs) pairing large VLMs with action heads and world-action models (WAMs) that jointly predict future observations and actions have become mainstream. Yet because these models vary parameter scale, pretraining data, and architecture simultaneously, prior literature could not attribute performance gains to any single factor—whether model scaling or pretraining priors.

To address this, the authors cleanly factorize manipulation policies into a representation extractor $f_{\phi}$ and a conditional action generator $p_{\theta}$. They fix the action generator to a compact Flow Matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that learns straight generative trajectories, allowing them to systematically vary properties of the representation extractor one by one.

Their testbed is CoRP, an intentionally compact model with only 48.9M (~0.05B) parameters. Despite having no VLM backbone or video-generative model, CoRP achieves a state-of-the-art 97.0% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, matching systems tens to over a hundred times larger. From this starting point, the authors conduct a series of rigorous intervention experiments to uncover why such a small policy works so well.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Generative Policies and Visual Representations
sections.summary: The paper surveys generative policies like Diffusion Policy alongside self-supervised visual representations like DINOv2. While prior work focused on frozen features or single-task setups, this study comprehensively explores representation properties in multi-task, language-conditioned generative policies.
sections.details:
In recent imitation learning, methods that use generative models as action heads, such as Diffusion Policy and ACT, have established strong baselines. However, they are traditionally trained on individual tasks. While models like Octo extended this to multi-task regimes, they learn visual tokenizers directly from robot data rather than fully harnessing large-scale pretrained image models.

On the other hand, recent VLAs and WAMs inherit rich pretrained representations, but their language models and parameter counts balloon at the same time, obscuring the true contribution of the visual representation itself.

### Positioning Within Visual Representation Learning
On the visual encoder side, the field has shifted from supervised ImageNet pretraining to self-supervised learning like DINOv2, which captures fine-grained patch-level features. While pretraining on human videos for robotics has also been explored, most works evaluate frozen features on single-task settings. This study distinguishes itself by unifying how pretraining initialization, fine-tuning, and token compression interact within multi-task, language-conditioned generative policies.

sections.heading: Designing CoRP: A Stripped-Down Policy Architecture
sections.summary: CoRP combines four standard components: a DINOv2 visual encoder, a tiny T5 language encoder, a learned query resampler, and a 1-block DiT action generator. It is trained end-to-end with a Flow Matching loss and an auxiliary task classification objective.
sections.details:
CoRP is designed to be as simple as possible, minimizing unnecessary moving parts.

### 3.1 Policy Architecture
The model consists of the following components:
- **Visual Encoder**: Each camera view is processed independently by a ViT-S/14 initialized with DINOv2. The resulting 256 patch tokens from a 224×224 image are fine-tuned end-to-end with the policy.
- **Language Encoder**: For short instruction prompts, it uses the minimal T5-Efficient-Tiny. The pooled text embedding $\bar{\mathbf{u}}$ is injected into both the resampler and the action generator.
- **Resampler (Vision-Language Fusion)**: Since 256 patch tokens per view are too heavy for action generation, a learned cross-attention resampler compresses them down to 48 tokens per view ($K=48$). The queries are FiLM-modulated by the text embedding $\bar{\mathbf{u}}$, selecting visual features conditioned on the instruction. Concatenating proprioceptive state tokens yields the conditioning representation $\mathbf{z}_t$.
- **Action Generator**: A single-block ($L=1$) DiT with a hidden width of 768. It takes noisy action chunks and $\mathbf{z}_t$, predicting action trajectories while applying text-conditioned adaptive layer normalization (adaLN) in each block.

### 3.2 Training Objective
Training uses a Flow Matching loss to predict the velocity field of action chunks. To ensure the resampled visual prefix retains critical task information, an auxiliary task classification loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}$ is added during training with a weight of $\lambda=0.01$.

captions.F1: Policy architecture of CoRP. Features extracted from vision, language, and proprioception are compressed into a compact token sequence via a resampler and fed into a minimal DiT-based action generator.

sections.heading: What Actually Matters? An Element-by-Element Investigation
sections.summary: Alongside benchmarks on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, the authors conduct rigorous ablations on encoder initialization, freezing, language conditioning, and information bottlenecks, followed by real-world dual-arm robot evaluations.
sections.details:
### 4.2 Can It Match Giant Systems?
On LIBERO, CoRP (0.049B) achieves an average success rate of 97.0%, directly matching the 3.3B $\pi_{0.5}$ (96.9%) and 7.0B OpenVLA-OFT (97.1%). On the dual-arm RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, CoRP scores 75.8% (Clean) and 73.4% (Randomized), significantly outperforming $\pi_{0.5}$ (43.0% / 43.8%), which is roughly 160× larger.

### 4.3 Is Pretrained Initialization Really Necessary?
Comparing DINOv2-initialized ViT-S/14 against ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 and their random counterparts reveals that DINOv2 ViT dominates at 97.0%, far ahead of random ViT (78.1%) and ImageNet ResNet (74.5%). Interestingly, all models achieve 100% task classification accuracy, yet manipulation success diverges sharply. This shows that DINOv2 provides the fine-grained spatial representations essential for physical manipulation, beyond just broad semantic task recognition.

### 4.4 Can We Just Freeze the Pretrained Encoder?
Freezing the encoder weights drops LIBERO performance from 97.0% down to 77.2%—a 19.8-point drop that puts it on par with a fully trained random ViT (78.1%). Linear probing and t-SNE visualizations (Figure F2) show that task adaptation is necessary to organize action-relevant features according to episode progress.

### 4.5 Is Language Conditioning Always Required?
Completely removing language conditioning destroys performance on LIBERO-Goal (where different goals share the same initial visual state), dropping it from 95.8% to 9.2%. However, on suites where the scene appearance uniquely identifies the goal, performance barely changes. On RoboTwin 2.0, removing language actually improves success by 2.7 points. Language does not inject general semantic knowledge; it simply disambiguates visually ambiguous goals.

### 4.6 Which Information Bottleneck Works Best?
The authors compare compressing 256 tokens down to 48 via the resampler (a hard token budget) against a variational information bottleneck (VIB; a continuous KL penalty). Passing all patch tokens drops performance to 83.2%, while adding a VIB collapses LIBERO-Goal to 33.0%. Uniform, task-agnostic compression penalizes the instruction-dependent visual selection the policy relies on.

### 4.7 Does It Work on Real Hardware?
CoRP was validated on a physical dual-arm robot across cup grasping, spoon placement, and charger plug insertion. When a human moved the cup or plate mid-execution, the policy updated its trajectory in the very next action chunk, successfully completing all 8 disturbance trials (Figure F3).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Remaining Challenges
sections.summary: The paper shows that compact policies require visual representations that are pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed. However, limitations remain regarding evaluation on closed task sets and the scope of real-world experiments.
sections.details:
Through the 48.9M-parameter CoRP, this work demonstrates that manipulation policy performance stems primarily from visual representation quality. Removing pretraining, task adaptation (fine-tuning), or token compression results in a 14 to 20 point drop on LIBERO. Furthermore, failing policies still understand what task they are performing; what they lack is not semantic task knowledge, but fine-grained spatial information needed for manipulation.

However, the authors highlight several limitations:
- **Evaluation on Closed Task Sets**: Benchmarks evaluate in-distribution control and do not test the open-world zero-shot generalization targeted by large VLAs and WAMs.
- **Attribution of Pretraining Benefits**: Without a supervised ViT baseline, the study cannot fully isolate whether gains stem specifically from DINOv2 self-supervised patch learning or ViT architecture priors.
- **Scope of Hardware Validation**: Real-world evaluation is limited to three demonstration tasks and lacks the exhaustive ablations conducted in simulation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training Dynamics and Latent Space Insights
sections.summary: The appendix details inference latency and ablation setups, while highlighting latent space collapse without language (t-SNE) and the counterintuitive disconnect between training loss and policy performance.
sections.details:
### Latent Space Separation via Language
t-SNE visualizations of feature representations with and without language (Figure F7) show that language conditioning yields well-separated task clusters. Without language, tasks in LIBERO-Goal—which share identical visual scenes—collapse into a single cluster. This confirms that language acts as a switch to disambiguate identical observations.

### The Pitfall of Training Loss
The appendix tracks training loss across ablations. Remarkably, the highest-performing configuration achieved the highest training loss on the logs. In policy learning, monitoring training loss alone fails to reflect policy quality; instead, directly tracking whether representations preserve action-critical information is essential.

### Inference Latency
Benchmarked on an Nvidia RTX 5090 without specialized optimization, CoRP achieves an inference latency of just 7.01 ms per action chunk. Its compact footprint comfortably supports high-frequency closed-loop control.

captions.F7: t-SNE visualization of visual prefixes across LIBERO suites with language (top) and without language (bottom), colored by task ID. Without language, the LIBERO-Goal suite (red box) completely collapses into a single indistinct cluster.

takeaways: The decisive driver of manipulation success is not model parameter scale, but a visual encoder that is pretrained, task-adapted, and properly compressed.
Freezing the visual encoder causes a severe performance penalty (~20 points); fine-tuning the vision backbone end-to-end with the policy is essential.
Compressing patch tokens to a compact budget using a language-modulated cross-attention resampler outperforms feeding all raw patch tokens directly into the policy.
Language conditioning is critical primarily when disambiguating multiple goals from identical visual states, rather than providing general world knowledge.
limitations: Evaluations are restricted to closed task sets like LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, without measuring open-world zero-shot generalization targeted by large VLAs.
The absence of a supervised ViT baseline leaves open whether benefits arise strictly from DINOv2 self-supervised pretraining or ViT architectures in general.
Physical robot experiments are limited to qualitative demonstrations across three tasks without exhaustive real-world ablations or baseline comparisons.
